title: NADE: neural conditionals & weight tying
blurb: Replace logistic regression with a one-hidden-layer network

hook.title: Private rulebooks vs a shared notebook
hook.text: In FVSBN every pixel has its **own private rulebook**: pixel 500 needs 500 numbers, pixel 501 needs 501 new ones. NADE says: let each rulebook be a tiny neural net, and let them **share one notebook** (the weight matrix $W$ and bias $c$). The notebook grows by a column per pixel, but pixels reuse what's already written, so you need far fewer numbers and can reuse earlier calculations.
hook.recall: Remember the shared notebook: tying the weights across pixels cuts parameters and speeds computation; only the little output layer ($\alpha_i,b_i$) stays pixel-specific.

explore.intro: Compare how parameter counts grow. FVSBN is from the slide; the NADE count is my extra bookkeeping for hidden size $d$.
tasks: Set $n=784$. How many parameters does FVSBN need?
Increase $d$. At what $n$ does tied-NADE become cheaper than FVSBN for $d=500$?
explore.takeaway: FVSBN ≈ $n^2/2$ parameters. NADE uses a hidden layer $h_i=\sigma(W_{<i}x_{<i}+c)$ with **tied** $W$, $c$: growth is linear in $n$ for fixed $d$.

options: W_{<i} x_{<i} + c  (tied weights, earlier pixels only)
W x_i + c  (the current pixel)
W x + c  (all pixels incl. later ones)
α_i h_i + b_i  (pixel-specific output layer)
W h_i  (no bias)
h_i x_i

build.explanation: NADE: $h_i=\sigma(W_{<i}x_{<i}+c)$ and $\hat x_i=p(x_i|x_{<i})=\sigma(\alpha_ih_i+b_i)$. The hidden layer only sees earlier pixels, so the DAG structure is preserved.

questions.prompt: How does NADE differ from FVSBN?
options: It uses a one-hidden-layer neural network instead of logistic regression for each conditional
It removes the chain rule
It samples all pixels in parallel
It only works for continuous data
questions.explanation: NADE keeps the same autoregressive chain rule; each conditional becomes a small neural net.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of **tying weights** in NADE?
options: It reduces the number of parameters and speeds up computation
It makes the model non-autoregressive
It lets pixels see later pixels
It guarantees better samples
questions.explanation: The shared notebook: one $W$ (and $c$) reused for all pixels.

questions.prompt: In FVSBN, how many parameters does the conditional for pixel $i=100$ have (bias + weights on earlier pixels)?
questions.explanation: $\alpha_0^i$ plus $i-1=99$ weights $=100$, which is why the total is $1+2+\dots+n$.

questions.prompt: FVSBN on a 784-pixel binary image: total parameters $1+2+\dots+784$?
Which statement about NADE is FALSE?
options: $h_i=\sigma(W_{<i}x_{<i}+c)$
$\hat x_i=\sigma(\alpha_ih_i+b_i)$
NADE produces all conditionals in one forward pass
Weight tying reduces the parameter count
questions.explanation: The slide on MADE points out that NADE requires **n passes**, while MADE gets all parameters in one pass: a motivation for masking.

questions.prompt: *“Tying the weights means every pixel has exactly the same conditional distribution.”* What’s the mistake?
options: Nothing
Only $W$ and $c$ are shared. Pixel $i$ uses its own earlier pixels $x_{<i}$ and its own output weights $\alpha_i,b_i$, so the conditionals differ
Tied weights make the conditionals independent of $x$
Tied weights break the chain rule
questions.explanation: Shared notebook, but each pixel reads a different page range and writes with its own pen.
